doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Juke joints, concert halls and stereotypes about drugs
summary: He says jazz was always elevated music, regardless of venue, and rejects drug stereotypes of its players.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well at the same point you can play music for a little five year old and they’ll start dancing. Until we bring it off of the lofty stools that there are, and heights, because we’re trying to offset the juke joints that the music thrived in. But whoever goes to Lincoln Center or Kennedy Center, the music you’re playing at Kennedy Center was played at those juke joints. So putting it behind a different building doesn’t change the music. If it’s elevated enough to be considered for the Kennedy Center then it was always elevated. Regardless of where they —because sometimes maybe that’s all the place they had to play the music. Okay? You can’t condemn the music because you see it in a juke joint or see people boozing or on drugs. Okay? Or of equating jazz musicians with being drug users, as though no other profession does it. So no one can convince me that the person that works in the stock market is not on drugs. Okay? All that yelling and screaming when the stock market changes. You’ve got to be on something. But they don’t get condemned.
